title: Check yourself: Use Cases for Sealed Classes and Interfaces

questions.stem: `upload(file)` used to throw an unchecked exception when the user was over quota. It now returns a sealed `UploadResult` that permits `Stored(url)` and `OverQuota(limitBytes)`. Four callers were changed, and none of them handles `OverQuota`. Which caller fails to compile?

options.text: `String msg = switch (upload(file)) { case Stored s -> "saved"; };`, since a switch expression over the sealed type must cover every permitted subtype or have a `default`.
options.says: The page's Forgot.java switch names only Success and javac reports that it does not cover all possible input values.

options.text: `upload(file);` on a line of its own, since a returned sealed value must be read by the caller before the statement ends.
options.says: The page shows charge("4120"); compiling without a warning, even under -Xlint:all.

options.text: `if (upload(file) instanceof Stored s) show(s.url());`, since an `instanceof` test against a sealed type needs an `else` for the other subtypes.
options.says: The page says an instanceof with no else compiles, like a dropped result.

options.text: `switch (upload(file)) { case Stored s -> show(s.url()); default -> { } }`, since a `default` is refused in a switch whose selector is a sealed type.
options.says: The page's simplify ends its rule switch over the sealed Expr with default -> walked, and that program compiled and ran.

origin.section: A Sealed Result Makes an Expected Failure a Value the Caller Has to Match

questions.stem: A `Priority` enum (`LOW`, `NORMAL`, `URGENT`) gets a mutable field `String escalatedBy`, set when an incident is raised to `URGENT`. Incident 1 is escalated by the night shift, then incident 2 by the day shift. What does incident 1 report as `escalatedBy`?

options.text: "day shift", since both incidents refer to the one `URGENT` instance, and the second assignment replaced the first.
options.says: The page's SharedConstant run: the second order's tracking number overwrote the first's, because a constant is one shared instance.

options.text: "night shift", since each incident that is set to `URGENT` holds a copy of the constant with its own fields.
options.says: A constant is one shared instance; the page's run shows the first order seeing the second's value.

options.text: Nothing: javac refuses the field, since a field declared in an enum must be `final` and set in the constructor.
options.says: The page's enum with a plain String trackingNo field compiled and ran.

options.text: Nothing: javac refuses the assignment, since an enum constant is a compile-time constant whose fields are read-only.
options.says: The page's run assigns first.trackingNo and second.trackingNo and prints the result.

origin.section: An Enum Is Still the Right Choice When a Variant Carries No Data

questions.stem: A sealed abstract `ImportException` permits `BadHeader`, `BadRow` and `Timeout`. `importFile()` declares `throws ImportException` and handles the three in three catch clauses. A release adds `Duplicate` to the `permits` list, and the parser starts throwing it. What happens?

options.text: It compiles, and a `Duplicate` leaves `importFile()` unhandled, since javac checks a switch against the `permits` list but never a set of catch clauses.
options.says: The page's clause version compiled after FraudHold was added, and the fraud hold escaped it at run time.

options.text: It compiles, and a `Duplicate` is caught by the last clause, since a sealed base sends a subtype nobody named to the closest clause.
options.says: The page's run shows FraudHold escaping the clauses, not handled by any of them.

options.text: javac refuses `importFile()`, since catch clauses over a sealed exception must name every permitted subtype, as a switch must.
options.says: After FraudHold was added javac reported only the switch; the page says it doesn't treat clauses as covering the sealed base.

options.text: javac refuses the parser's `throw`, since a new permitted subtype must be caught by name wherever its base is caught.
options.says: javac reported only the switch inside the one catch; nothing else in the program was refused.

origin.section: A Sealed Exception Hierarchy Lets One catch Answer Every Failure, and a New One Breaks the Build

questions.stem: A billing library returns invoices that are either drafts or issued. Callers in other packages must be able to switch over the two kinds without a `default`, and must never create an issued invoice themselves. Which layout does both?

options.text: Public sealed interfaces `Draft` and `Issued`, each permitting a package-private record, since callers can name the interfaces in cases but can't implement them or reach the records.
options.says: This is the page's Tracking layout: callers switch over the public sub-interfaces, an implementation of their own is refused, and the records are hidden.

options.text: Public sealed interfaces `Draft` and `Issued`, each permitting a public record, since a permitted record's constructor can only be called from the package of its sealed interface.
options.says: The page says public records fail because anyone can call their constructor.

options.text: Package-private records `Draft` and `Issued` under one public sealed interface, since callers can match on records they can't construct.
options.says: The page's Peek.java shows javac refusing a package-private record named from another package: not public in shipping.

options.text: Public records `Draft` and `Issued` under one public sealed interface, since sealing the interface also stops other packages from constructing its records.
options.says: Sealing limits which classes implement the interface, not who calls a public record's constructor; the page says public records fail the second rule.

origin.section: Public Sealed Interfaces Over Package-Private Records Let Callers Match but Not Implement
